title: Ordinary Differential Equations
subject: Mathematics

cards.prompt: What is Ordinary Differential Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ordinary differential equation relates an unknown function of one independent variable to its ordinary derivatives. The unknown may be scalar- or vector-valued; partial derivatives in several independent variables belong to PDEs instead.
required_concepts: Unknown function of one independent variable.
Relation involves ordinary derivatives.
accepted_variants: An equation governing a function through derivatives with respect to one variable.
major_error_concepts: Classifying an equation with essential partial derivatives in several variables as an ODE.

cards.prompt: What is Order of an ODE? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The order of an ODE is the highest derivative order that appears effectively in the equation. A second-order equation involves a second derivative and no higher derivative.
required_concepts: Highest derivative order, not a polynomial exponent.
accepted_variants: The number of differentiations in the highest derivative present.
major_error_concepts: Calling a first derivative squared a second-order derivative.

cards.prompt: What is Degree of an ODE? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The degree of an ODE, when defined, is the polynomial degree of its highest-order derivative after the equation has been written polynomially in its derivatives without changing the relevant solution relation. Many nonpolynomial derivative relations have no degree in this sense.
required_concepts: Polynomial degree of the highest-order derivative.
Not defined for every ODE.
accepted_variants: Highest-derivative exponent in an appropriate polynomial derivative relation.
major_error_concepts: Confusing degree with derivative order.

cards.prompt: What is Explicit ODE? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An explicit ODE is solved for its highest derivative, such as x' = f(t,x) or x'' = f(t,x,x'). Its right-hand side may still depend nonlinearly on the lower derivatives and unknown function.
required_concepts: Highest derivative isolated.
Explicit does not imply linear.
accepted_variants: Normal-form differential equation.
major_error_concepts: Calling an equation explicit only when its solution formula is already known.

cards.prompt: What is Implicit ODE? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An implicit ODE specifies a relation F(t,x,x',...,x^(n)) = 0 without necessarily isolating the highest derivative. Solving it locally for that derivative may require an implicit-function condition and may fail at singular points.
required_concepts: Derivative relation not necessarily solved for the highest derivative.
accepted_variants: An ODE given as a constraint among the variables and derivatives.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every implicit equation has one globally equivalent explicit form.

cards.prompt: What is Linear ODE? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A linear ODE is linear in the unknown function and its derivatives, with coefficients depending only on the independent variable. Products or nonlinear functions of the unknown and its derivatives violate linearity.
required_concepts: Unknown and derivatives enter linearly.
Coefficients may depend on the independent variable.
accepted_variants: A linear differential operator applied to the unknown equals a given forcing.
major_error_concepts: Calling x' = x squared linear because only a first derivative appears.

cards.prompt: What is Nonlinear ODE? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A nonlinear ODE fails linearity in its unknown function or derivatives. Examples include x' = x squared and x'' + sin x = 0; derivative order and nonlinearity are separate classifications.
required_concepts: Nonlinear dependence on the unknown or its derivatives.
accepted_variants: An equation outside the linear differential-operator form.
major_error_concepts: Classifying an equation as nonlinear merely because its coefficient is sin t.

cards.prompt: What is Autonomous ODE? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An autonomous ODE has no explicit dependence on the independent time variable, as in x' = f(x). Solutions may vary in time even though the vector field itself does not explicitly do so.
required_concepts: Right-hand side independent of time explicitly.
Does not mean solutions are constant.
accepted_variants: A time-independent vector field.
major_error_concepts: Calling every time-varying solution nonautonomous.

cards.prompt: What is Nonautonomous ODE? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A nonautonomous ODE depends explicitly on time, such as x' = f(t,x) with genuine t dependence. The same state can have a different instantaneous derivative at different times.
required_concepts: Explicit dependence of the equation on time.
accepted_variants: A time-dependent vector field.
major_error_concepts: Calling x' = x nonautonomous because x depends on t.

cards.prompt: What is Initial Value Problem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An initial value problem consists of a differential equation and values of the unknown and required lower derivatives at one initial point. For x' = f(t,x), the datum is x(t0) = x0.
required_concepts: Differential equation plus data at one initial point.
accepted_variants: An ODE with an initial state.
major_error_concepts: Confusing data imposed at two distinct endpoints with a standard initial value problem.

cards.prompt: What is Boundary Value Problem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A boundary value problem imposes constraints on a solution at boundary points, often two endpoints of an interval. Unlike a regular IVP, compatible boundary data may yield no solution, one solution, or many.
required_concepts: Conditions imposed at interval boundaries.
Existence and uniqueness differ from IVP theory.
accepted_variants: An ODE with endpoint boundary conditions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming any pair of endpoint values automatically determines a unique solution.

cards.prompt: What is Solution of an ODE? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A classical solution of an ODE is a sufficiently differentiable function on an interval that satisfies the equation at each point and satisfies any stated data. Its domain is part of the solution specification.
required_concepts: Required differentiability and pointwise satisfaction.
Include the interval and supplied data.
accepted_variants: A function satisfying the differential relation on its domain.
major_error_concepts: Accepting a formula through a point where it is undefined as a solution on the entire interval.

cards.prompt: What is Maximal Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A maximal solution is one that cannot be extended to a strictly larger interval while remaining a solution of the same problem. Maximal does not imply that its domain is all real time or that its values are largest.
required_concepts: No proper solution extension to a larger interval.
Maximal interval may be finite.
accepted_variants: A solution continued as far as the equation and domain permit.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting maximal as largest numerical solution value.

cards.prompt: What is Solution Extension? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An extension of a solution is a solution on a larger interval that agrees with the original on its entire interval. The extension must satisfy the same ODE and retain the original data.
required_concepts: Larger interval with agreement on the original domain.
accepted_variants: Continuation of a solution beyond its current interval.
major_error_concepts: Calling any unrelated solution on a larger interval an extension.

cards.prompt: What is Phase Space? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Phase space is the space of possible state vectors needed to specify the evolution. A second-order scalar equation is commonly represented with state (x,x'), so its phase space is two-dimensional.
required_concepts: States contain enough variables for first-order evolution.
Dimension need not equal the number of physical position coordinates.
accepted_variants: State space for the dynamical system.
major_error_concepts: Using position alone as the full state for a general second-order equation.

cards.prompt: What is Flow? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For an autonomous ODE with unique solutions, a flow maps an initial state to its state after elapsed time: phi_t(x0). Where defined it satisfies phi_0 = identity and phi_(t+s) = phi_t composed with phi_s.
required_concepts: Time evolution of initial states under an autonomous equation.
Composition law holds on the common domain.
accepted_variants: The solution-generated family of state maps.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a local flow is automatically defined for every real time.

cards.prompt: What is First-Order IVP Notation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A first-order IVP written x'(t) = f(t,x(t)), x(t0) = x0 specifies both the instantaneous evolution rule and the initial state. For vector x, the same notation represents a coupled first-order system.
required_concepts: Differential evolution rule and initial value.
x can be a state vector.
accepted_variants: Normal-form first-order initial value problem.
major_error_concepts: Treating f(t,x) as an already integrated solution.

cards.prompt: What is Separable Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A separable first-order equation has the form x' = g(t)h(x). Away from zeros of h, variables can be separated and integrated; equilibria at zeros of h must be retained separately.
required_concepts: Product of a time-only and a state-only factor.
Division may lose constant solutions.
accepted_variants: An ODE reducible to dx/h(x) = g(t) dt where division is valid.
major_error_concepts: Dividing by h(x) and discarding all solutions where h vanishes.

cards.prompt: What is Linear First-Order Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A linear first-order scalar equation can be written x' + p(t)x = q(t). The coefficients depend only on time, and an integrating factor transforms it into a derivative of a product.
required_concepts: Standard form x' + p x = q.
p and q depend only on the independent variable.
accepted_variants: An inhomogeneous first-order linear differential equation.
major_error_concepts: Including x-dependent p in the standard linear form.

cards.prompt: What is Integrating Factor? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For x' + p(t)x = q(t), an integrating factor is a nonzero function mu(t) = exp(integral p(t) dt). Multiplication gives (mu x)' = mu q.
required_concepts: Choose mu with mu' = p mu.
The left side becomes a product derivative.
accepted_variants: An exponential multiplier making the linear equation directly integrable.
major_error_concepts: Using exp(integral q dt) as the standard integrating factor.

cards.prompt: What is Exact Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A differential equation M(t,x) dt + N(t,x) dx = 0 is exact when the left side is dPhi for a potential Phi. Its solution curves lie on level sets Phi(t,x) = constant, subject to local regularity.
required_concepts: Differential form is a total differential.
Solutions follow potential level sets.
accepted_variants: An equation admitting Phi_t = M and Phi_x = N.
major_error_concepts: Calling every separable-looking differential form exact without checking its coefficients.

cards.term: Potential Function for an Exact ODE
cards.prompt: What is Potential Function for an Exact ODE? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The potential of an exact first-order differential form is a scalar function Phi with partial derivatives Phi_t = M and Phi_x = N. It is determined up to an additive constant on a connected domain.
required_concepts: Gradient components reproduce the form coefficients.
Additive constant does not change the differential form.
accepted_variants: A primitive whose total differential is M dt + N dx.
major_error_concepts: Confusing this mathematical potential automatically with physical potential energy.

cards.prompt: What is Bernoulli Substitution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Bernoulli equation x' + p(t)x = q(t)x^n with n not zero or one becomes linear in v = x^(1-n) wherever the substitution is defined. Zeros and domain restrictions require separate consideration.
required_concepts: Power substitution v = x^(1-n).
Substitution linearizes the Bernoulli form on a valid domain.
accepted_variants: Reduction of Bernoulli's nonlinear first-order equation to a linear one.
major_error_concepts: Using the substitution across forbidden powers or division by zero without checking solutions.

cards.prompt: What is Riccati Substitution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a Riccati equation x' = a(t)x squared + b(t)x + c(t), knowing one particular solution x_p permits the substitution x = x_p + 1/u, which yields a linear first-order equation for u where u is nonzero.
required_concepts: Quadratic first-order Riccati form.
Known particular solution enables a linearizing reciprocal shift.
accepted_variants: Riccati reduction using x_p + 1/u.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the substitution requires no known particular solution.

cards.prompt: What is Homogeneous-Type Substitution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a first-order equation x' = F(x/t), the substitution v = x/t, so x = tv and x' = v + tv', reduces it to tv' = F(v) - v where t is nonzero. This homogeneous-type terminology differs from a homogeneous linear equation.
required_concepts: Ratio substitution x = tv.
Distinguish scaling-homogeneous form from linear homogeneous equations.
accepted_variants: A ratio-dependent equation reduced by a scaling substitution.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every homogeneous-type equation is linear.

cards.prompt: What is Singular Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A singular solution is a solution not obtained as an ordinary member of a specified general solution family. It can arise as an envelope or be lost by a division or substitution; the term should be tied to the equation and family in question.
required_concepts: Solution outside the stated general family.
Must still satisfy the original differential equation.
accepted_variants: An exceptional solution missed by the regular family or reduction.
major_error_concepts: Calling an undefined or non-solution formula singular merely because it diverges.

cards.prompt: What is Equilibrium Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An equilibrium solution of x' = f(x) is a constant x(t) = x_star with f(x_star) = 0. Equilibria are fixed states of the autonomous dynamics.
required_concepts: Constant solution at a zero of the vector field.
accepted_variants: Stationary solution or fixed point.
major_error_concepts: Calling a point where x momentarily stops an equilibrium when f does not vanish there.

cards.prompt: What is Separable Reduction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Separation reduces x' = g(t)h(x) to integral dx/h(x) = integral g(t) dt on intervals where h is nonzero. The resulting implicit relation and any excluded equilibrium solutions together describe the candidate solutions.
required_concepts: Separate and integrate on a valid interval.
Retain solutions excluded by division.
accepted_variants: Variable separation with domain and equilibrium bookkeeping.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every integration constant selects a globally defined solution.

cards.prompt: What is Integrating-Factor Method? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The integrating-factor method rewrites x' + p x = q as (mu x)' = mu q, then integrates to obtain x = mu^-1(C + integral mu q dt). Initial data fix the integration constant.
required_concepts: Product derivative after multiplication.
Divide by the nonzero integrating factor after integration.
accepted_variants: Linear first-order solution by an integrating multiplier.
major_error_concepts: Integrating q alone after multiplying the left side by mu.

cards.prompt: What is Exactness Criterion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For continuously differentiable M and N on a simply connected domain, M_x = N_t ensures M dt + N dx is exact. Recover a potential by integrating one component and determining the missing single-variable function from the other.
required_concepts: Cross-partial equality with suitable domain assumptions.
Reconstruction must satisfy both potential derivatives.
accepted_variants: Exactness test plus recovery of a scalar primitive.
major_error_concepts: Treating cross-partial equality as a global exactness guarantee on every punctured domain.

cards.prompt: What is Local Existence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Local existence means at least one solution of an IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. It does not by itself guarantee uniqueness or continuation for all time.
required_concepts: Existence on a neighborhood of the initial time.
Separate existence from uniqueness and global continuation.
accepted_variants: A solution exists for sufficiently small elapsed time.
major_error_concepts: Inferring a unique global solution solely from local existence.

cards.prompt: What is Global Existence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Global existence means the solution exists throughout the specified full time range, often all forward time or all real time. Local existence alone does not prevent finite-time blow-up or departure from the equation's domain.
required_concepts: Existence over the stated global time range.
Meaning of global must specify forward or two-sided time.
accepted_variants: Continuation without finite-time obstruction on the target range.
major_error_concepts: Calling a solution global simply because a closed-form expression is available.

cards.prompt: What is Local Uniqueness? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Local uniqueness means two solutions of the same IVP agree on a sufficiently small common interval near the initial time. It is a property of the differential equation and data under specified regularity conditions.
required_concepts: Same initial data imply local agreement.
Uniqueness is distinct from existence.
accepted_variants: There is at most one local solution through the prescribed initial point.
major_error_concepts: Assuming continuity of f alone always gives uniqueness.

cards.prompt: What is Local Lipschitz Condition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A vector field is locally Lipschitz in x when, near each relevant point, |f(t,x)-f(t,y)| <= L|x-y| with a local constant uniform over the considered time neighborhood. This controls state sensitivity strongly enough for standard local uniqueness results.
required_concepts: Local linear bound on differences in f with respect to state.
The relevant bound is locally uniform in time.
accepted_variants: Locally bounded state-space difference quotient.
major_error_concepts: Equating mere continuity with local Lipschitz continuity.

cards.prompt: What is Maximal Interval of Existence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The maximal interval of existence is the largest connected time interval containing the initial time to which a solution can be continued. A finite endpoint can reflect unbounded state growth or approach to the boundary of the vector field's domain.
required_concepts: Largest continuation interval for the given solution.
Finite endpoints need not be singularities of the independent variable alone.
accepted_variants: The domain of the maximally continued solution.
major_error_concepts: Extending through a pole by pretending the formula remains differentiable there.

cards.prompt: What is Finite-Time Blow-Up? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Finite-time blow-up means that a solution exists up to a finite endpoint T but its state norm becomes unbounded as t approaches T from within its existence interval. Failure to continue because a bounded trajectory reaches the boundary of the vector field's domain is a broader domain-escape phenomenon, not automatically norm blow-up. For x'=x² with x(0)=1, x(t)=1/(1-t) blows up at T=1.
required_concepts: The maximal endpoint T is finite.
The state norm is unbounded as the endpoint is approached.
Bounded domain-boundary escape alone is not norm blow-up.
major_error_concepts: A solution tending to the finite value 1 at the boundary of the domain (-1,1) necessarily has norm blow-up.

cards.prompt: What is Well-Posedness? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An IVP is well posed in a specified setting when a solution exists, is unique, and depends continuously on the supplied data in the chosen topology. The time interval and admissible data class are part of the statement.
required_concepts: Existence, uniqueness, and continuous dependence.
Specify the setting and interval.
accepted_variants: Hadamard well-posedness of the evolution problem.
major_error_concepts: Calling a problem well posed based on existence alone.

cards.prompt: What is Continuous Dependence on Initial Data? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Continuous dependence on initial data means nearby initial states produce nearby solutions on a specified common time interval, under the relevant regularity assumptions. It need not prevent large separation over very long times.
required_concepts: Closeness of data yields closeness of trajectories on the specified interval.
accepted_variants: Finite-time solution sensitivity is continuous in initial state.
major_error_concepts: Inferring that nearby initial conditions remain arbitrarily close forever.

cards.prompt: What is Continuous Dependence on Parameters? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Continuous dependence on parameters means small changes in equation parameters yield small changes in solutions on a specified common interval under suitable assumptions. The result concerns finite-time behavior, not automatic preservation of asymptotic attractors.
required_concepts: Solution varies continuously with the equation parameter.
State the common time interval.
accepted_variants: Finite-time continuity of the parameter-to-solution map.
major_error_concepts: Assuming continuous finite-time dependence rules out bifurcations in long-time behavior.

cards.prompt: What is Picard Iteration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Picard iteration constructs successive approximations x_(k+1)(t) = x0 + integral from t0 to t of f(s,x_k(s)) ds. Under suitable Lipschitz and interval bounds, the sequence converges to the IVP solution.
required_concepts: Iterate the integral equation using the previous approximation.
Convergence requires appropriate local hypotheses.
accepted_variants: Successive approximations for the IVP integral operator.
major_error_concepts: Replacing the previous iterate inside f with an unknown final solution and calling that an iteration.

cards.prompt: What is Peano Existence Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Peano's existence theorem gives local existence for a finite-dimensional IVP when the vector field is continuous near the initial point. It does not in general give uniqueness.
required_concepts: Continuity yields local existence.
Uniqueness is not part of this conclusion.
accepted_variants: Local existence under continuity without a Lipschitz uniqueness assumption.
major_error_concepts: Attributing uniqueness to Peano's theorem under continuity alone.

cards.prompt: What is IVP Integral Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For continuous f, a solution of x' = f(t,x), x(t0) = x0 satisfies x(t) = x0 + integral from t0 to t of f(s,x(s)) ds. Conversely a continuous function satisfying this integral equation is differentiable and solves the IVP.
required_concepts: Integral equation encodes both derivative and initial value.
Equivalence uses continuity of the integrand.
accepted_variants: Integral formulation of the first-order IVP.
major_error_concepts: Omitting x0 or changing the integration lower limit without adjusting the constant.

cards.prompt: What is Picard–Lindelof Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Picard-Lindelof gives a unique local solution when f is continuous in time and locally Lipschitz in state near the initial point, with the local bound uniform over the time neighborhood. Global existence needs additional continuation control.
required_concepts: Continuity and local state-Lipschitz hypotheses.
Conclusion is local existence and uniqueness.
accepted_variants: The standard local existence-uniqueness theorem for regular IVPs.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the local theorem alone ensures existence for all time.

cards.prompt: What is Autonomous Scalar Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An autonomous scalar ODE has one real state variable and form x' = f(x). Its sign determines the local direction of motion along a one-dimensional state line.
required_concepts: One scalar state and no explicit time dependence.
accepted_variants: One-dimensional autonomous dynamics.
major_error_concepts: Calling a two-state planar autonomous system scalar.

cards.prompt: What is Phase Line? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A phase line marks equilibria and signs of f(x) for x' = f(x). Arrows indicate increasing or decreasing state between equilibria and help infer stability without solving the equation explicitly.
required_concepts: Equilibria and directional arrows from the sign of f.
A state-space sketch, not a position-time graph.
accepted_variants: One-dimensional qualitative dynamics diagram.
major_error_concepts: Reading the horizontal phase-line coordinate as time.

cards.prompt: What is Stable Equilibrium? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An equilibrium x* of an autonomous ODE is Lyapunov stable if for every epsilon>0 there is delta>0 such that solutions starting within delta of x* remain within epsilon of x* for all t≥0. Under the usual local existence and uniqueness assumptions, the nearby solutions in this definition must exist for all those future times. Stability does not by itself require convergence to x*; attraction is an additional condition.
required_concepts: Every prescribed epsilon has a sufficiently small initial delta.
Closeness persists for all future time, not just a fixed finite horizon.
Convergence to the equilibrium is not part of stability alone.
major_error_concepts: An equilibrium is Lyapunov stable whenever nearby trajectories remain close for the first ten seconds, even if they then move far away.

cards.prompt: What is Unstable Equilibrium? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An equilibrium is unstable when the stability condition fails: some fixed neighborhood cannot retain all sufficiently nearby initial states for forward time. Instability need not mean every nearby state moves away monotonically.
required_concepts: Failure of Lyapunov stability.
At least some arbitrarily close data escape a fixed neighborhood.
accepted_variants: A fixed point that is not stable.
major_error_concepts: Requiring every nearby trajectory to diverge in order to call an equilibrium unstable.

cards.prompt: What is Asymptotically Stable Equilibrium? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An equilibrium is asymptotically stable if it is stable and attracts all states in some neighborhood as time tends to infinity. Attraction alone is not the full definition without stability.
required_concepts: Stability plus local convergence to the equilibrium.
accepted_variants: A locally stable attracting fixed point.
major_error_concepts: Defining asymptotic stability solely as bounded motion nearby.

cards.prompt: What is Invariant Interval? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An interval is positively invariant when every solution starting in it remains in it for future time. For regular scalar equations, vector-field directions at its endpoints can establish that trajectories cannot exit.
required_concepts: Forward trajectories stay in the interval.
Endpoint directions must be compatible with no outward crossing.
accepted_variants: A forward-invariant range of scalar states.
major_error_concepts: Calling an interval invariant merely because it contains an equilibrium.

cards.prompt: What is Basin of Attraction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The basin of attraction of an attracting equilibrium is the set of initial states whose forward solutions converge to it. It can extend far beyond the neighborhood used in a local stability theorem.
required_concepts: Set of initial states converging to the same attractor.
accepted_variants: Attraction domain.
major_error_concepts: Confusing the basin with the single equilibrium point.

cards.prompt: What is Noncrossing under Uniqueness? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: When an autonomous IVP has unique solutions, distinct trajectories cannot cross in phase space and then follow different futures. For nonautonomous equations, equality of state at different times is not the same initial-value event.
required_concepts: Same state at the same time has a unique continuation.
Phase-space noncrossing requires the appropriate autonomous or time-augmented setting.
accepted_variants: Uniqueness prevents branching of solution trajectories.
major_error_concepts: Forbidding two nonautonomous solutions from visiting the same state at different times.

cards.prompt: What is Sign and Monotonicity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For x' = f(x), positive f makes a solution increase and negative f makes it decrease while it remains in that sign region. At zeros of f, equilibria must be considered with the relevant uniqueness assumptions.
required_concepts: Sign of f sets direction of scalar motion.
accepted_variants: Positive derivative gives increasing state and negative derivative decreasing state.
major_error_concepts: Using the sign of x itself instead of the sign of f(x) to infer motion.

cards.prompt: What is Phase-Line Qualitative Analysis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a regular autonomous scalar ODE, equilibria and sign intervals often determine qualitative future behavior through monotonicity and barriers. Existence limits and the state domain still matter; phase-line reasoning is not a guarantee of global existence.
required_concepts: Use sign intervals and equilibria to infer qualitative trajectories.
Respect possible finite-time escape and domain endpoints.
accepted_variants: Global qualitative analysis from one-dimensional flow directions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every arrow toward infinity takes infinite time to get there.

cards.prompt: What is Euler Method? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Forward Euler approximates x' = f(t,x) by x_(n+1) = x_n + h f(t_n,x_n). It uses the slope at the beginning of each step and is a first-order method under standard smoothness and stability conditions.
required_concepts: Advance with the current slope.
First-order global accuracy under appropriate conditions.
accepted_variants: Explicit Euler time stepping.
major_error_concepts: Evaluating the new-state slope and still calling the method forward Euler.

cards.prompt: What is Local Truncation Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Local truncation error measures the one-step defect when a numerical step begins from the exact solution. An unnormalized local defect for a method of global order p is typically O(h^(p+1)); conventions dividing by h instead report O(h^p).
required_concepts: One-step error from exact starting data.
State whether the defect is normalized by step size.
accepted_variants: The numerical method's single-step consistency error.
major_error_concepts: Equating local error with the accumulated numerical error after many steps.

cards.prompt: What is Global Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Global error is the difference between the numerical state and the exact solution at a mesh point after accumulated time stepping. It reflects both local defects and how the method propagates earlier errors.
required_concepts: Numerical-minus-exact error at a computed time.
Accumulation and propagation matter.
accepted_variants: Total solution error over a finite integration interval.
major_error_concepts: Assuming global error equals one isolated step's truncation error.

cards.prompt: What is Consistency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A numerical ODE method is consistent when its local defect vanishes at the required rate as step size tends to zero, so the discrete update approximates the differential equation. Consistency alone does not guarantee stable long-run propagation.
required_concepts: Small-step update approximates the ODE.
Separate consistency from stability.
accepted_variants: Vanishing local discretization defect.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a consistent scheme is automatically accurate at arbitrarily large step sizes.

cards.prompt: What is Numerical Stability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Numerical stability concerns control of perturbation and error amplification under repeated updates. Its precise meaning depends on the setting, such as finite-interval stability or absolute stability on the test equation x' = lambda x.
required_concepts: Control of perturbation propagation.
The relevant stability notion must be specified.
accepted_variants: Bounded or appropriately controlled amplification by the discrete method.
major_error_concepts: Confusing numerical stability with physical equilibrium stability in every context.

cards.prompt: What is Numerical Convergence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A numerical method converges on a fixed interval when its maximum mesh-point error tends to zero as the step size tends to zero. Convergence order describes the rate under stated regularity and stability assumptions.
required_concepts: Global error tends to zero on the specified fixed interval.
accepted_variants: The discrete solution approaches the exact solution as the mesh is refined.
major_error_concepts: Calling one visually plausible coarse-grid trajectory proof of convergence.

cards.prompt: What is Step Size? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Step size h is the time increment between successive mesh points. Smaller steps usually reduce discretization error but increase work, and stability restrictions may impose an upper limit depending on the equation and method.
required_concepts: Time increment of the discretization.
Accuracy, stability, and computational cost all depend on it.
accepted_variants: Time-step length.
major_error_concepts: Claiming halving the step always halves every source of numerical error.

cards.prompt: What is One-Step Method? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A one-step method computes the next state from the current state and time, possibly using intermediate evaluations, without requiring a history of earlier solution states. Euler and Runge-Kutta methods are examples.
required_concepts: Next update uses the current state rather than a multistep state history.
accepted_variants: A numerical integrator with a one-state update map.
major_error_concepts: Calling Runge-Kutta multistep solely because it has several internal stages.

cards.prompt: What is Runge–Kutta Method? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Runge-Kutta method forms one time-step update from a weighted combination of slope evaluations at internal stage points. Stage coefficients determine the method's order and stability properties.
required_concepts: Multiple stage slopes combined in one update.
Order is not determined by stage count alone.
accepted_variants: A staged one-step integration method.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every four-stage method is automatically fourth-order.

cards.prompt: What is Forward Euler Update? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The update x_(n+1) = x_n + h f(t_n,x_n) extrapolates the current tangent over one step. Its explicit character means no equation for x_(n+1) must be solved inside that update.
required_concepts: Current slope times step is added to current state.
No implicit new-state solve.
accepted_variants: Forward Euler's update rule.
major_error_concepts: Replacing the slope with f(t_(n+1),x_(n+1)) and calling it the same explicit update.

cards.prompt: What is Consistency–Stability–Convergence Principle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For regular one-step ODE methods on a fixed interval, consistency together with suitable stability bounds yields convergence. The stability bound controls how the accumulated local defects affect the global error.
required_concepts: Consistency and appropriate stability are both needed.
Conclusion applies under the stated regularity and fixed-interval setting.
accepted_variants: Stable accumulation of vanishing local defects produces a vanishing global error.
major_error_concepts: Dropping all assumptions and applying the slogan to arbitrary numerical algorithms.

cards.prompt: What is Local versus Global Error Order? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a stable order-p method over a fixed interval, an unnormalized per-step defect O(h^(p+1)) typically accumulates over O(1/h) steps into global error O(h^p). This uses smoothness and controlled error amplification.
required_concepts: One-step defect typically has one extra power of h.
Global estimate needs stability and a fixed time range.
accepted_variants: Local order p+1 and global order p under the unnormalized-defect convention.
major_error_concepts: Assuming an O(h squared) one-step defect makes Euler globally second-order.

cards.prompt: What is Gronwall and Numerical Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Gronwall estimate bounds numerical error recurrences or inequalities by accumulated local forcing times an exponential amplification factor. It connects local defects with finite-time global-error control when the field is Lipschitz.
required_concepts: Bounds propagated error using an integral or discrete inequality.
Amplification depends on a Lipschitz-type bound.
accepted_variants: Gronwall controls accumulation and amplification of numerical defects.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the estimate prevents all long-time exponential separation.

cards.prompt: What is Linear Differential Operator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A linear differential operator maps x to a linear combination of its derivatives, Lx = sum a_k(t)x^(k). It obeys L(alpha u + beta v) = alpha Lu + beta Lv.
required_concepts: Linear combination of derivatives with time-dependent coefficients.
Preserves linear combinations.
accepted_variants: A derivative-based linear map on functions.
major_error_concepts: Including products such as x x' in a linear operator.

cards.prompt: What is Homogeneous Linear Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A homogeneous linear ODE has the form Lx = 0. Its solutions form a vector space, unlike the solution set of a general nonzero-forcing equation.
required_concepts: Zero right-hand side for a linear operator.
Solution set closed under linear combinations.
accepted_variants: The zero-forcing associated linear equation.
major_error_concepts: Confusing linear homogeneity with a nonlinear ratio-dependent homogeneous-type equation.

cards.prompt: What is Nonhomogeneous Linear Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A nonhomogeneous linear ODE has the form Lx = g with specified forcing g not identically zero. Its solutions differ from each other by solutions of the associated homogeneous equation.
required_concepts: Specified nonzero forcing.
Differences of solutions satisfy Lx = 0.
accepted_variants: An inhomogeneous linear equation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a sum of two solutions to the same nonzero-forcing equation solves that same equation.

cards.prompt: What is Fundamental Set of Solutions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A fundamental set for a regular nth-order homogeneous linear ODE consists of n linearly independent solutions spanning its solution space on the interval. Every homogeneous solution is their constant-coefficient linear combination.
required_concepts: n independent solutions for an order-n regular equation.
They span the homogeneous solution space.
accepted_variants: A basis of homogeneous solutions.
major_error_concepts: Using dependent solutions as a fundamental set.

cards.prompt: What is Linear Independence of Functions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Functions are linearly independent on an interval when a constant-coefficient combination vanishes identically only if every coefficient is zero. Dependence concerns equality over the interval, not at just one point.
required_concepts: Only the trivial constant-coefficient combination is identically zero.
accepted_variants: No function lies in the constant linear span of the others.
major_error_concepts: Declaring functions dependent because they share a zero at one point.

cards.prompt: What is Wronskian? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Wronskian of n functions is the determinant with columns containing each function and its derivatives through order n-1. A nonzero value proves independence; stronger zero-versus-nonzero conclusions require additional assumptions, such as a common regular linear ODE.
required_concepts: Determinant of functions and successive derivatives.
Nonzero Wronskian implies independence; zero alone is subtler for arbitrary functions.
accepted_variants: A derivative determinant testing a candidate fundamental family.
major_error_concepts: Claiming an identically zero Wronskian proves dependence for every arbitrary differentiable family.

cards.prompt: What is Complementary Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The complementary solution is the general solution of the homogeneous equation associated with a nonhomogeneous linear ODE. Adding a particular solution yields the full nonhomogeneous family.
required_concepts: General homogeneous part of the solution.
accepted_variants: Complementary function.
major_error_concepts: Calling one forced solution the complementary solution.

cards.prompt: What is Particular Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A particular solution is one specified function satisfying a nonhomogeneous linear equation. It contains no requirement to span all solutions; different choices differ by a homogeneous solution.
required_concepts: One solution of the forced equation.
Not the whole general family.
accepted_variants: One representative in the affine nonhomogeneous solution set.
major_error_concepts: Demanding that a particular solution alone satisfy every possible initial condition.

cards.prompt: What is Superposition Principle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a linear operator, homogeneous solutions can be combined with constant coefficients to produce another homogeneous solution. More generally, combining solutions with different forcings combines the forcings by the same coefficients.
required_concepts: Linearity carries combinations of solutions to combinations of forcing.
Same zero forcing is preserved in the homogeneous case.
accepted_variants: Superposition of linear responses.
major_error_concepts: Applying unrestricted solution superposition to nonlinear equations.

cards.prompt: What is Reduction of Order? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Reduction of order uses a known nonzero solution y1 of a second-order homogeneous linear equation and seeks another as y = v y1. Substitution reduces the remaining task to an equation of lower order on intervals where the construction is valid.
required_concepts: Use y = v y1 with one known solution.
Reduces order on an appropriate interval.
accepted_variants: Construct a second solution from a known first one.
major_error_concepts: Treating the multiplier v as necessarily constant.

cards.prompt: What is Variation of Parameters? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Variation of parameters seeks a forced linear solution as a combination of homogeneous basis solutions with time-dependent coefficients. Auxiliary conditions give equations for those coefficient derivatives and hence a particular solution.
required_concepts: Replace constant homogeneous coefficients by functions.
Use a fundamental family to construct a forced response.
accepted_variants: Variation of constants in a homogeneous solution basis.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the variable coefficients are arbitrary after the forcing equation is imposed.

cards.term: Dimension of the Homogeneous Solution Space
cards.prompt: What is Dimension of the Homogeneous Solution Space? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A regular nth-order homogeneous linear scalar ODE has an n-dimensional solution space on its interval. The standard assumptions include continuous normalized coefficients and a nonvanishing leading coefficient before normalization.
required_concepts: Dimension equals order under regular linear-ODE hypotheses.
Leading coefficient must not vanish on the interval.
accepted_variants: n independent initial data parameterize the homogeneous solution space.
major_error_concepts: Applying the dimension statement unchanged through singular leading-coefficient zeros.

cards.prompt: What is Homogeneous plus Particular Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: If x_p is one solution of Lx = g, every solution is x = x_h + x_p with Lx_h = 0. This follows because subtracting two forced solutions cancels the forcing.
required_concepts: General solution equals homogeneous solution plus one particular solution.
accepted_variants: Affine translate of the homogeneous solution space.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying a particular solution by an arbitrary constant while keeping the forcing unchanged.

cards.prompt: What is Characteristic Polynomial Method? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a constant-coefficient homogeneous linear ODE, substituting e^(rt) gives a characteristic polynomial. A root r of multiplicity m contributes t^k e^(rt) for k from zero to m-1; complex conjugate roots combine into real exponential-sinusoidal solutions.
required_concepts: Exponential ansatz leads to the characteristic polynomial.
Repeated roots require polynomial factors.
accepted_variants: Characteristic-root construction of a fundamental family.
major_error_concepts: Using only one exponential for a repeated root and claiming a complete basis.

cards.prompt: What is Abel's Wronskian Formula? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For y'' + p(t)y' + q(t)y = 0, the Wronskian satisfies W' = -pW, hence W(t) = W(t0) exp(-integral from t0 to t of p(s) ds). It is either nowhere zero or identically zero on a regular interval.
required_concepts: Wronskian satisfies the scalar first-order equation W' = -pW.
Conclusion holds on an interval of regular coefficients.
accepted_variants: Abel's identity for a second-order linear equation.
major_error_concepts: Using q rather than p in the Wronskian exponential.

cards.prompt: What is Harmonic Oscillator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A harmonic oscillator satisfies x'' + omega0 squared x = 0 with omega0 positive. Its solutions are sinusoidal combinations with constant amplitude in the ideal unforced, undamped model.
required_concepts: Linear restoring equation with positive squared frequency.
Sinusoidal undamped free motion.
accepted_variants: The simple linear oscillator.
major_error_concepts: Calling every periodic nonlinear motion exactly harmonic.

cards.prompt: What is Oscillator Damping? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In m x'' + c x' + k x = 0 with m and k positive, positive c models viscous damping. The discriminant c squared - 4mk distinguishes underdamped, critically damped, and overdamped motion.
required_concepts: Positive velocity-proportional resistance.
Damping regime depends on the characteristic roots.
accepted_variants: Energy-dissipating linear oscillator resistance.
major_error_concepts: Assuming positive damping always permits oscillation.

cards.prompt: What is Oscillator Forcing? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Forcing is a prescribed external input on the right-hand side of an ODE, such as F(t) in m x'' + c x' + k x = F(t). It drives a response in addition to free homogeneous motion.
required_concepts: Given external input.
Distinguish forced response from homogeneous motion.
accepted_variants: An inhomogeneous driving term.
major_error_concepts: Calling initial displacement itself a continuing external force.

cards.prompt: What is Natural Frequency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The natural angular frequency of an ideal mass-spring oscillator is omega0 = sqrt(k/m). It describes undamped free motion and differs from the damped oscillation frequency when damping is present.
required_concepts: Undamped free-oscillation angular frequency.
omega0 = sqrt(k/m).
accepted_variants: The oscillator's unforced undamped characteristic frequency.
major_error_concepts: Equating natural frequency with any imposed drive frequency.

cards.prompt: What is Resonance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Resonance is an enhanced response when a drive interacts with an oscillatory mode near its characteristic frequency. A sinusoidally forced undamped linear oscillator at exact resonance has secular amplitude growth; damping limits the steady-state response and can shift its peak.
required_concepts: Drive couples strongly near a modal frequency.
Distinguish ideal undamped growth from damped finite response.
accepted_variants: Frequency-selective amplification of forced oscillation.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every damped resonant response grows without bound.

cards.prompt: What is Beats? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Beats are slow amplitude modulations produced by superposing oscillations with nearby frequencies. For equal-amplitude cosines, the product identity separates a rapid carrier from a slow envelope associated with their frequency difference.
required_concepts: Superposition of nearby frequencies.
Slow amplitude modulation differs from the rapid oscillation.
accepted_variants: Interference envelope between close-frequency oscillations.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting beats as evidence of dissipative damping by themselves.

cards.prompt: What is Transient Response? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The transient response is the part of a solution associated with initial conditions that disappears with time in a stable dissipative linear system. In such a system it is represented by decaying homogeneous modes.
required_concepts: Initial-condition contribution that decays under stability assumptions.
accepted_variants: The decaying free response before long-time forced behavior dominates.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every homogeneous solution decays even in an unstable or undamped system.

cards.prompt: What is Steady-State Response? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A steady-state response is the persistent long-time response to sustained forcing after decaying transients vanish. For a stable linear oscillator under sinusoidal forcing it is a sinusoid at the drive frequency with an amplitude and phase shift.
required_concepts: Persistent response after stable transients decay.
Need not be a constant value.
accepted_variants: Long-time forced response.
major_error_concepts: Equating steady state with zero time derivative in every forced system.

cards.prompt: What is Quality Factor? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a lightly damped linear oscillator, the quality factor Q measures weak damping and sharp frequency selectivity. With m x'' + c x' + k x = 0, Q = m omega0/c; it is also approximately 2 pi times stored energy divided by energy lost per cycle in the weak-damping regime.
required_concepts: Dimensionless measure of damping and resonance sharpness.
State the weak-damping condition for the cycle-loss interpretation.
accepted_variants: High Q means relatively small fractional energy loss per oscillation.
major_error_concepts: Claiming high Q means stronger damping.

cards.prompt: What is Forced Damped Oscillator Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The equation m x'' + c x' + k x = F(t) balances inertia, linear viscous resistance, and linear restoring force against an external drive. Standard mechanical interpretations take m positive, k positive, and c nonnegative.
required_concepts: Identify inertia, damping, stiffness, and forcing terms.
State the linear model assumptions.
accepted_variants: The forced damped mass-spring equation.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting c x' as the spring displacement force.

cards.prompt: What is Ordinary Point? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a normalized second-order linear equation y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = 0, an ordinary point is one where p and q are analytic in a neighborhood. Power-series solution theory applies there.
required_concepts: Normalized coefficients analytic near the point.
accepted_variants: A nonsingular analytic point of the linear equation.
major_error_concepts: Calling a point ordinary without first accounting for a vanishing leading coefficient.

cards.prompt: What is Singular Point? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A singular point of a linear ODE is a point where the normalized coefficient conditions for an ordinary point fail. It may arise from dividing by a leading coefficient that vanishes there.
required_concepts: Failure of the normalized ordinary-point regularity.
accepted_variants: A point where the equation is not ordinary in the analytic-coefficient sense.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every solution must diverge at every singular point.

cards.prompt: What is Regular Singular Point? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = 0, x0 is regular singular when (x-x0)p(x) and (x-x0) squared q(x) extend analytically near x0, even though x0 is singular. These controlled poles permit Frobenius theory.
required_concepts: Weighted coefficients extend analytically.
Second-order weights are first and second powers respectively.
accepted_variants: A singularity mild enough for the standard Frobenius framework.
major_error_concepts: Requiring p and q themselves to be analytic and thereby confusing regular singular with ordinary.

cards.prompt: What is Irregular Singular Point? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An irregular singular point is a singular point that fails the regular-singular conditions. The local solution behavior may require techniques beyond ordinary Frobenius power series, such as asymptotic expansions.
required_concepts: Singular but not regular singular.
accepted_variants: A singularity outside the regular-singular class.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the usual indicial polynomial always completely describes irregular-singular behavior.

cards.prompt: What is Power-Series Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A power-series solution represents the unknown as sum a_n(x-x0)^n near a point. Substituting into the ODE and matching coefficients determines recurrence relations and free coefficients corresponding to initial data.
required_concepts: Series representation about a center.
Coefficient matching gives recurrence relations.
accepted_variants: Local analytic solution construction by a Taylor-type series.
major_error_concepts: Treating a formal recurrence as proof of convergence without suitable analytic conditions.

cards.prompt: What is Radius of Convergence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The radius of convergence is the radius of the interval or complex disk where a power series converges absolutely about its center. For analytic ODE solutions, singularities of the normalized equation constrain the region guaranteed by local analytic theory, though individual solutions may extend farther.
required_concepts: Convergence distance from the expansion center.
Distinguish guaranteed coefficient-domain bounds from a particular solution's possible extension.
accepted_variants: The maximal open disk of power-series convergence.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every coefficient singularity must be a singularity of every solution.

cards.prompt: What is Frobenius Method? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Frobenius method seeks y = (x-x0)^r sum a_n(x-x0)^n near a regular singular point, with a0 nonzero. The exponent is selected by an indicial equation; a second independent solution may require logarithmic terms.
required_concepts: Power factor times analytic series.
Indicial exponents and possible logarithmic companion solution.
accepted_variants: Generalized power-series construction at a regular singular point.
major_error_concepts: Guaranteeing two plain Frobenius series for every pair of indicial roots.

cards.prompt: What is Indicial Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The indicial equation is the algebraic condition on the leading exponent r obtained from the lowest-power term of a Frobenius substitution. Its roots guide the possible local solution forms near a regular singular point.
required_concepts: Lowest-order balance determines the exponent.
Root relations influence companion solution form.
accepted_variants: The characteristic equation for Frobenius exponents.
major_error_concepts: Confusing it with the constant-coefficient characteristic polynomial in all cases.

cards.prompt: What is Ordinary-Point Series Principle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: At an ordinary point of a linear ODE with analytic normalized coefficients, the IVP has a local analytic solution represented by a convergent power series. The required initial values determine the free series coefficients.
required_concepts: Analytic normalized coefficients yield local analytic solutions.
Initial data determine the appropriate coefficients.
accepted_variants: Ordinary-point analytic existence for linear equations.
major_error_concepts: Claiming smooth but nonanalytic coefficients automatically yield convergent Taylor solutions.

cards.prompt: What is Regular-Singular Solution Forms? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: At a regular singular point, Frobenius theory provides local solution forms based on indicial exponents. Depending on repeated roots or integer root differences, a second solution can involve logarithms rather than another independent plain power-factor series.
required_concepts: Regular singularity permits Frobenius-type construction.
Logarithmic terms may be needed.
accepted_variants: Regular-singular local solution classification.
major_error_concepts: Discarding a logarithmic solution simply because it is not a pure power series.

cards.prompt: What role do special-function families play as ODE solutions, and must every member be non-elementary?
cards.definition: Standard differential equations define named solution families, such as Bessel, Airy, and Legendre functions. They extend the useful library beyond elementary formulas, but a special function need not be non-elementary: for certain parameters, Legendre solutions include polynomials. Boundary conditions and normalization determine which member or combination solves a particular problem.
required_concepts: Named solution families arise from standard ODEs.
Special-function status does not imply every member is non-elementary.
Parameters and boundary or normalization conditions matter.
major_error_concepts: No Legendre polynomial can count as a special function because it has an elementary polynomial expression.

cards.prompt: What is First-Order ODE System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A first-order system x' = f(t,x) evolves a vector of state variables whose derivatives may depend on one another. A higher-order scalar ODE can be rewritten as such a system by including lower derivatives in the state.
required_concepts: Vector-valued first-order evolution.
Higher-order equations can be converted to first-order systems.
accepted_variants: Coupled first-order state equations.
major_error_concepts: Treating coupled coordinates as independent scalar IVPs without their coupling terms.

cards.prompt: What is Linear System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A linear first-order system has the form x' = A(t)x + g(t), with a time-dependent matrix A and prescribed forcing vector g. Linearity concerns state dependence, not whether A is constant.
required_concepts: Matrix-linear state dependence plus prescribed forcing.
accepted_variants: A vector linear differential equation.
major_error_concepts: Calling a system nonlinear solely because its matrix varies with time.

cards.prompt: What is Homogeneous Linear System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A homogeneous linear system is x' = A(t)x with zero forcing. Its solution set is a vector space and a fundamental matrix can propagate any initial state.
required_concepts: Zero forcing in a linear system.
accepted_variants: The unforced matrix differential equation.
major_error_concepts: Calling a system homogeneous merely because its matrix is constant.

cards.prompt: What is Inhomogeneous Linear System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An inhomogeneous linear system is x' = A(t)x + g(t) with a prescribed nonzero forcing vector. Its general solution consists of a homogeneous solution plus any one particular solution.
required_concepts: Nonzero prescribed forcing vector.
Homogeneous-plus-particular structure.
accepted_variants: A forced linear system.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a linear combination of same-forcing solutions retains that same forcing without coefficient restrictions.

cards.prompt: What is Fundamental Matrix? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A fundamental matrix Phi(t) has linearly independent homogeneous solution vectors as its columns. It satisfies Phi' = A(t)Phi and is invertible throughout a regular solution interval.
required_concepts: Independent solution columns.
Invertible matrix satisfying the homogeneous matrix equation.
accepted_variants: A matrix-valued solution basis.
major_error_concepts: Calling any singular collection of solution columns a fundamental matrix.

cards.prompt: What is Matrix Exponential? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The matrix exponential exp(At) is defined by the convergent series sum (At)^k/k!. For constant A it satisfies d exp(At)/dt = A exp(At) and exp(A0) = I, including when A is not diagonalizable.
required_concepts: Series definition and constant-matrix evolution property.
Does not require diagonalizability.
accepted_variants: The exponential propagator for a constant linear system.
major_error_concepts: Exponentiating each matrix entry independently and calling that the matrix exponential.

cards.prompt: What is Variation of Constants? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Variation of constants for x' = A(t)x + g(t) uses a fundamental matrix Phi to give x(t) = Phi(t)[Phi(t0)^-1 x0 + integral from t0 to t of Phi(s)^-1 g(s) ds]. It separates homogeneous propagation from accumulated forcing.
required_concepts: Fundamental matrix propagates both initial data and transformed forcing.
Inverse matrix acts at the integration time inside the integral.
accepted_variants: The system-level variation-of-parameters formula.
major_error_concepts: Removing the inverse fundamental matrix from the forcing integral without justification.

cards.prompt: What is Jordan Blocks and Linear Dynamics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Jordan-form viewpoint decomposes constant-matrix dynamics into eigenvalue growth or decay together with polynomial factors from nilpotent Jordan blocks. A size-m block can generate powers through t^(m-1) multiplying an exponential.
required_concepts: Eigenvalue exponentials plus polynomial factors for defective blocks.
Diagonalization is not always possible.
accepted_variants: Generalized eigenvectors describe non-diagonalizable linear evolution.
major_error_concepts: Dropping all polynomial factors when a matrix has a nontrivial Jordan block.

cards.prompt: What is Homogeneous Matrix-Exponential Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For x' = Ax with constant matrix A and x(t0) = x0, the solution is x(t) = exp(A(t-t0))x0. The formula handles coupled coordinates and does not require A to be diagonalizable.
required_concepts: Constant A and the time difference t-t0.
Multiply the initial vector by the matrix exponential.
accepted_variants: Constant-coefficient homogeneous system solution.
major_error_concepts: Using exp(At)x0 while ignoring a nonzero initial time.

cards.prompt: What is Forced Matrix-Exponential Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For constant A, the forced solution is x(t) = exp(A(t-t0))x0 + integral from t0 to t of exp(A(t-s))g(s) ds. Each forcing contribution is propagated from its application time s to the observation time t.
required_concepts: Initial propagation plus convolution-type forcing integral.
Kernel depends on t-s.
accepted_variants: Duhamel or variation-of-constants formula for constant A.
major_error_concepts: Replacing exp(A(t-s)) by exp(At) inside the integral in general.

cards.prompt: What is Phase Portrait? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A phase portrait depicts solution trajectories in state space for an autonomous system, often together with equilibria and direction arrows. It displays geometric evolution rather than plotting every state coordinate against time.
required_concepts: Trajectories in phase space.
Direction and qualitative structures characterize dynamics.
accepted_variants: State-space picture of a dynamical system.
major_error_concepts: Reading a closed orbit as a constant equilibrium merely because it closes in space.

cards.prompt: What is Nullcline? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A nullcline is a set where one component of a planar vector field vanishes. On an x-nullcline x' = 0 but y' may be nonzero; intersections of all component nullclines are equilibrium candidates.
required_concepts: One derivative component vanishes.
A single nullcline need not consist of equilibria.
accepted_variants: A zero-component curve of the planar field.
major_error_concepts: Calling every point of one nullcline a full equilibrium.

cards.prompt: What is Invariant Set? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A set is positively invariant if trajectories starting in it remain there for forward time. Full invariance includes both forward and backward evolution wherever the flow is defined.
required_concepts: State the time direction of invariance.
Trajectories do not leave the set in that direction.
accepted_variants: A set preserved by the flow.
major_error_concepts: Equating forward invariance with two-sided invariance without additional assumptions.

cards.prompt: What is Trajectory? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A trajectory or orbit is the set traced in phase space by a solution as time varies. The parameterized solution includes timing information that the geometric orbit alone may omit.
required_concepts: State-space path generated by a solution.
Distinguish geometry from time parameterization.
accepted_variants: The flow path through an initial state.
major_error_concepts: Assuming identical geometric orbits always imply identical speeds along them.

cards.prompt: What is Omega-Limit Set? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The omega-limit set of a forward trajectory consists of state-space limit points reached along sequences of times tending to infinity. For a precompact trajectory in a regular flow, it is nonempty and compact.
required_concepts: Accumulation points along times going to positive infinity.
Nonemptiness needs conditions such as precompactness.
accepted_variants: The set of possible long-time accumulation states.
major_error_concepts: Defining it as the set of all states visited at any finite time.

cards.prompt: What is Attractor? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An attractor is an invariant set that attracts a specified neighborhood or class of initial states under the adopted definition. Attractors may be equilibria, periodic orbits, or more complicated sets; stability and minimality conventions should be stated when needed.
required_concepts: Invariant attracting set.
Need not be a single point.
accepted_variants: A set approached by nearby or otherwise specified forward trajectories.
major_error_concepts: Calling any one point temporarily approached by a trajectory an attractor.

cards.prompt: What is Repeller? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A repeller is an invariant set that attracts nearby trajectories under reversed time in the appropriate local setting, or equivalently repels them forward under corresponding assumptions. It is not merely any equilibrium with one unstable direction.
required_concepts: Invariant set with backward attraction or suitable forward repulsion.
A saddle need not be a repeller.
accepted_variants: A time-reversed attractor.
major_error_concepts: Equating every unstable equilibrium with a full repeller.

cards.prompt: What is Trapping Region? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A trapping region is a region that forward trajectories cannot leave, often established by a vector field pointing strictly inward on its boundary. A compact trapping region can confine long-time dynamics without identifying a unique attractor.
required_concepts: Forward confinement.
Inward boundary direction is a common sufficient condition.
accepted_variants: A region trapping future trajectories.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every trapping region contains exactly one equilibrium.

cards.prompt: What is Planar Vector Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A planar vector field assigns a velocity vector f(x,y) to each point of a two-dimensional state domain. Its integral curves satisfy x' = f1(x,y), y' = f2(x,y).
required_concepts: A velocity vector assigned at each planar state.
Integral curves follow those assigned directions.
accepted_variants: A two-dimensional autonomous differential system.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting the vector field as a position vector rather than the state's derivative.

cards.prompt: What is Lyapunov Stability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Lyapunov stability of an equilibrium means every sufficiently small permitted error in initial state remains small for all future time. Formally, each epsilon neighborhood has a delta neighborhood whose trajectories stay inside it.
required_concepts: Epsilon-delta forward-time closeness.
Convergence is not required.
accepted_variants: Persistent closeness under small initial perturbations.
major_error_concepts: Requiring nearby trajectories to converge in order to satisfy stability alone.

cards.prompt: What is Asymptotic Stability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An equilibrium is asymptotically stable when it is Lyapunov stable and nearby forward trajectories converge to it. The neighborhood of attraction can be local rather than all phase space.
required_concepts: Stability and attraction together.
Local need not mean global.
accepted_variants: A stable equilibrium with local asymptotic convergence.
major_error_concepts: Calling an equilibrium globally attracting based only on a local theorem.

cards.prompt: What is Exponential Stability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An equilibrium is exponentially stable when nearby deviations obey a bound |x(t)-x_star| <= C exp(-alpha(t-t0))|x0-x_star| with positive C and alpha. This provides a quantitative decay rate stronger than asymptotic stability alone.
required_concepts: Uniform local exponential decay bound.
Stronger than merely tending to zero.
accepted_variants: Stability with a controlled exponential convergence rate.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every asymptotically stable equilibrium converges exponentially.

cards.prompt: What is Linearization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Linearization approximates a differentiable autonomous system near equilibrium x_star by u' = Df(x_star)u for the small displacement u = x-x_star. Nonlinear remainder terms are higher order, but can matter when the linear part is inconclusive.
required_concepts: Jacobian gives the first-order local dynamics.
Zero-real-part eigenvalues can require nonlinear analysis.
accepted_variants: First-order Taylor approximation of the vector field at equilibrium.
major_error_concepts: Treating the linearized model as a globally exact system.

cards.prompt: What is Jacobian at Equilibrium? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Jacobian matrix Df(x_star) has entries partial f_i/partial x_j evaluated at the equilibrium. It records how each derivative component responds to small state perturbations.
required_concepts: Matrix of first state partial derivatives at the specified point.
accepted_variants: The derivative matrix of the vector field.
major_error_concepts: Using partial derivatives with respect to time in place of state derivatives for an autonomous Jacobian.

cards.prompt: What is Lyapunov Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Lyapunov function is a scalar function used to assess stability by its value and derivative along trajectories. Near an equilibrium, a positive-definite V with nonpositive trajectory derivative is a standard sufficient structure for stability.
required_concepts: Scalar measure positive away from equilibrium.
Derivative along solutions controls whether it decreases.
accepted_variants: An energy-like stability certificate without explicit integration.
major_error_concepts: Assuming any scalar function with a local minimum proves stability without checking its derivative along the flow.

cards.prompt: What is Differential Inequality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A differential inequality bounds a derivative rather than specifying it exactly, such as u' <= a(t)u+b(t). Comparison arguments turn such bounds into estimates on solutions, growth, or perturbations.
required_concepts: Derivative inequality used for comparison bounds.
accepted_variants: A differential relation bounding possible evolution.
major_error_concepts: Replacing an inequality by equality and claiming the resulting comparison function is the original solution.

cards.prompt: What is Gronwall Inequality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A basic Gronwall inequality states that if nonnegative u satisfies u(t) <= a + integral from t0 to t of b(s)u(s) ds, with a nonnegative and b nonnegative integrable, then u(t) <= a exp(integral b). It bounds accumulated feedback growth.
required_concepts: Integral inequality with nonnegative data.
Exponential upper bound.
accepted_variants: An exponential comparison estimate for an integral growth inequality.
major_error_concepts: Using the conclusion without accounting for the sign and integrability assumptions.

cards.prompt: What is Jacobian Eigenvalue Stability Test? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a continuously differentiable system near equilibrium, strictly negative real parts of all Jacobian eigenvalues imply local exponential stability. A positive-real-part eigenvalue implies instability; zero real parts make this test inconclusive in general.
required_concepts: Negative real parts imply local stability; a positive real part implies instability.
Zero-real-part cases need more analysis.
accepted_variants: The linearized eigenvalue stability test.
major_error_concepts: Declaring a nonlinear equilibrium stable solely because all real parts are nonpositive.

cards.prompt: What is Lyapunov Direct Method? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Lyapunov direct method proves stability using a positive-definite scalar V and its trajectory derivative Vdot = gradient V dot f. Nonpositive Vdot gives stability under standard local assumptions; negative-definite Vdot gives asymptotic stability with the appropriate neighborhood conditions.
required_concepts: Inspect V and its derivative along the actual vector field.
Distinguish nonpositive from negative-definite derivative conclusions.
accepted_variants: Stability analysis by a decreasing energy-like function.
major_error_concepts: Claiming Vdot <= 0 alone always gives asymptotic convergence without an additional argument.

cards.prompt: What is Parameter Sensitivity Estimate? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
