cards.definition: Parameter sensitivity estimates bound differences between solutions of nearby parameterized equations. Under state-Lipschitz and controlled parameter dependence, a Gronwall argument bounds finite-time solution differences by initial mismatch and parameter-induced forcing differences.
required_concepts: Compare two parameterized solutions on a common interval.
Include parameter forcing difference and error amplification.
accepted_variants: Quantitative finite-time dependence on equation parameters.
major_error_concepts: Inferring uniform infinite-time sensitivity control from a finite-interval estimate.

cards.prompt: What is Initial-Data Sensitivity Estimate? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: If f is L-Lipschitz in state on the relevant region, two solutions of the same equation satisfy |x(t)-y(t)| <= exp(L(t-t0))|x0-y0| over their common forward interval. This controls finite-time dependence without asserting contraction.
required_concepts: Initial separation multiplied by an exponential bound.
Positive L bound need not imply solutions actually diverge.
accepted_variants: Gronwall initial-condition sensitivity bound.
major_error_concepts: Treating the upper bound as an exact equality for every pair of solutions.

cards.prompt: What is Hartman–Grobman Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Hartman-Grobman theorem states that near a hyperbolic equilibrium of a sufficiently regular finite-dimensional autonomous system, the nonlinear flow is locally topologically conjugate to its linearization. Hyperbolic means no Jacobian eigenvalue has zero real part; the correspondence need not be differentiable.
required_concepts: Hyperbolic equilibrium requirement.
Local topological equivalence, not exact equality of nonlinear and linear solutions.
accepted_variants: Local qualitative dynamics match the hyperbolic linearization.
major_error_concepts: Applying the theorem at a center with purely imaginary eigenvalues.

cards.prompt: What is Periodic Orbit? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A periodic orbit is the phase-space path of a nonconstant solution satisfying x(t+T) = x(t) for some positive T. The same closed geometric path is traversed repeatedly.
required_concepts: Nonconstant solution repeating after a positive period.
accepted_variants: A closed orbit of the flow.
major_error_concepts: Counting an equilibrium as a nontrivial periodic orbit merely because its constant solution repeats.

cards.prompt: What is Limit Cycle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A limit cycle is an isolated periodic orbit: sufficiently nearby periodic orbits do not form a continuous family around it. It may be attracting, repelling, or have one-sided stability.
required_concepts: Periodic orbit isolated among periodic orbits.
Need not be attracting.
accepted_variants: An isolated closed orbit.
major_error_concepts: Calling every closed orbit around a linear center a limit cycle.

cards.prompt: What is Poincare–Bendixson Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A standard Poincare-Bendixson result says that for a continuously differentiable planar autonomous flow, a nonempty compact omega-limit set containing no equilibria is a periodic orbit under the usual planar hypotheses. It is a special restriction of two-dimensional flows, not a general higher-dimensional theorem.
required_concepts: Planar autonomous setting with compact omega-limit set.
No equilibria in that set leads to a periodic orbit.
accepted_variants: A bounded planar long-time limit without equilibria must be a closed orbit in the standard setting.
major_error_concepts: Applying the result unchanged to three-dimensional chaotic systems.

cards.prompt: What is Bendixson–Dulac Criterion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Bendixson-Dulac criterion rules out periodic orbits in a simply connected planar region when a suitable continuously differentiable multiplier B makes divergence of Bf strictly one sign throughout that region. It is a nonexistence criterion, not a recipe locating a cycle.
required_concepts: Signed divergence of a Dulac-weighted planar field.
Simply connected domain and regularity conditions.
accepted_variants: A one-sign divergence test excluding closed orbits.
major_error_concepts: Inferring a periodic orbit exists whenever the criterion fails.

cards.prompt: What is Two-Point Boundary Value Problem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A two-point boundary value problem imposes conditions at both ends of an interval, such as y(a)=alpha and y(b)=beta. Solvability depends on the equation, interval, and boundary operator, not just the number of conditions.
required_concepts: Data at two distinct endpoints.
Existence and uniqueness require separate analysis.
accepted_variants: An endpoint-constrained differential problem.
major_error_concepts: Applying an IVP uniqueness theorem directly to conclude every two-point BVP is uniquely solvable.

cards.prompt: What is Green's Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Green's function represents the response of a linear differential boundary problem to a point source while satisfying its boundary conditions. When the inverse exists, integrating G(x,s) against the forcing constructs the corresponding solution, with conventions set by the operator.
required_concepts: Impulse response for a specified linear operator and boundary conditions.
Integral representation requires appropriate solvability.
accepted_variants: The integral kernel of the linear boundary operator's inverse.
major_error_concepts: Using a Green's function for one boundary condition unchanged for an incompatible boundary condition.

cards.prompt: What is Self-Adjoint Operator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A self-adjoint differential operator equals its adjoint under a specified inner product and operator domain. Integration by parts and boundary conditions are essential; formal symmetry of the differential expression alone does not determine a self-adjoint boundary problem.
required_concepts: Equality to adjoint includes inner product and domain.
Boundary conditions matter.
accepted_variants: A symmetric differential expression realized with an appropriate self-adjoint domain.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring boundary terms and declaring any formally symmetric expression self-adjoint on every domain.

cards.prompt: What is Differential Eigenvalue Problem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An eigenvalue problem seeks scalars lambda and nonzero functions y satisfying Ly = lambda w y with specified boundary conditions. Boundary conditions restrict the permitted values and distinguish it from an unconstrained forced equation.
required_concepts: Nonzero eigenfunction and spectral parameter.
Boundary conditions are part of the problem.
accepted_variants: A differential operator's spectral problem.
major_error_concepts: Accepting the zero function as an eigenfunction for every lambda.

cards.prompt: What is Sturm–Liouville Problem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Sturm-Liouville problem has the form -(p y')' + q y = lambda w y with suitable boundary conditions. In the regular self-adjoint case on a finite interval, p and w are positive and the theory gives real eigenvalues and weighted orthogonality.
required_concepts: Self-adjoint second-order weighted eigenvalue form.
State regularity, positivity, and boundary assumptions for the spectral conclusions.
accepted_variants: A self-adjoint second-order boundary spectral problem.
major_error_concepts: Claiming arbitrary non-self-adjoint boundary conditions preserve all Sturm-Liouville conclusions.

cards.prompt: What is Eigenfunction Orthogonality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Eigenfunctions of a self-adjoint Sturm-Liouville problem with distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal in the weighted inner product: integral w y_m y_n = 0 in the real case. The weight is part of the problem and cannot generally be omitted.
required_concepts: Distinct eigenvalues imply weighted orthogonality.
Use the specified weight and self-adjoint boundary setting.
accepted_variants: Orthogonality under the Sturm-Liouville weight.
major_error_concepts: Claiming unweighted orthogonality when the problem has a nonconstant weight.

cards.prompt: What is IVP–BVP Distinction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Regular IVPs select a solution from data at one point, whereas BVPs impose constraints across an interval. Even a smooth linear equation can have no BVP solution or infinitely many at special parameters despite well-behaved IVP uniqueness.
required_concepts: Local initial data and distributed boundary constraints differ.
BVP nonuniqueness can occur without IVP nonuniqueness.
accepted_variants: Boundary solvability is a global constraint issue.
major_error_concepts: Using a successful IVP uniqueness result as proof that all boundary data are compatible.

cards.prompt: What is Spectral Modes and Function Expansions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Sturm-Liouville eigenfunctions provide mode bases for expansions used in Fourier analysis and separation-of-variables PDE methods. Orthogonality and appropriate completeness results permit projection onto modes under the relevant function-space assumptions.
required_concepts: Boundary eigenfunctions supply expansion modes.
Completeness and admissible function space require stated hypotheses.
accepted_variants: ODE spectral modes underpin Fourier-type and PDE expansions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every family of independent ODE solutions automatically forms a complete orthogonal basis.

cards.prompt: What is Hamiltonian System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A canonical Hamiltonian system satisfies q' = partial H/partial p and p' = -partial H/partial q. When H has no explicit time dependence, H is conserved along solutions under the usual differentiability assumptions.
required_concepts: Canonical paired equations with opposite sign.
Autonomous Hamiltonian is conserved.
accepted_variants: Phase-space dynamics generated by a Hamiltonian function.
major_error_concepts: Reversing one canonical sign or assuming explicitly time-dependent H must remain constant.

cards.prompt: What is Gradient System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A gradient system has form x' = -gradient V(x). Along its solutions, dV/dt = -|gradient V| squared <= 0, so V decreases except at critical points in the standard Euclidean setting.
required_concepts: Motion follows the negative gradient.
Potential is nonincreasing along trajectories.
accepted_variants: Gradient descent as continuous-time dynamics.
major_error_concepts: Claiming V increases under negative-gradient flow.

cards.prompt: What is Conserved Quantity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A conserved quantity I(x) is constant along solutions, so gradient I dot f = 0 for an autonomous differentiable system. Its level sets constrain trajectories without necessarily determining them completely.
required_concepts: Zero derivative along the flow.
Conservation restricts trajectories to level sets.
accepted_variants: A first integral of the differential system.
major_error_concepts: Calling a decreasing Lyapunov function a conserved quantity.

cards.prompt: What is Dissipative Flow? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A dissipative flow in the energy sense loses a specified energy-like quantity along trajectories. Other uses describe phase-volume contraction or existence of an absorbing set; these definitions are related in some models but should not be treated as universally equivalent.
required_concepts: Specify the intended meaning of dissipation.
Energy decay and phase-volume contraction are distinct notions.
accepted_variants: Dynamics with a stated loss or contraction property.
major_error_concepts: Inferring a specific energy law solely from negative divergence without defining that energy.

cards.prompt: What is Duffing Oscillator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Duffing oscillator is a nonlinear oscillator commonly written x'' + delta x' + alpha x + beta x cubed = gamma cos(omega t). The cubic restoring term permits amplitude-dependent behavior beyond the linear oscillator, with qualitative dynamics depending on parameters.
required_concepts: Cubic nonlinear restoring term.
Damping and periodic forcing are optional model components.
accepted_variants: A driven or undriven cubic-stiffness oscillator.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every Duffing parameter choice is chaotic.

cards.prompt: What is Forced Pendulum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A forced pendulum retains the nonlinear restoring term sin theta and adds external drive, often with damping: theta'' + c theta' + (g/L)sin theta = A cos(omega t). Large-angle and driven behavior can differ substantially from a linear small-angle oscillator.
required_concepts: Nonlinear sine restoring term with external forcing.
Small-angle linearization is a restricted approximation.
accepted_variants: A nonlinearly driven pendulum model.
major_error_concepts: Replacing sin theta by theta at arbitrary amplitude without an approximation statement.

cards.prompt: What is Lorenz System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Lorenz system is x' = sigma(y-x), y' = x(rho-z)-y, z' = xy-beta z. It is a three-dimensional autonomous nonlinear model that can exhibit chaotic dynamics for suitable parameters; chaos is not present for every parameter choice.
required_concepts: Three coupled autonomous nonlinear equations.
Chaotic behavior is parameter-dependent.
accepted_variants: The Lorenz convection-inspired dynamical system.
major_error_concepts: Claiming all three-dimensional ODEs or all Lorenz parameters are chaotic.

cards.prompt: What is Stable and Unstable Manifolds? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Near a hyperbolic equilibrium, stable and unstable invariant manifolds consist locally of states approaching the equilibrium in forward and backward time respectively. Their tangent spaces at the equilibrium are the stable and unstable eigenspaces of the linearization.
required_concepts: Invariant sets of forward or backward convergence.
Tangency to corresponding linearized eigenspaces under hyperbolicity.
accepted_variants: Nonlinear counterparts of stable and unstable linear subspaces.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the nonlinear manifolds are globally identical to the linear eigenspaces.

cards.prompt: What is Hopf Bifurcation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Hopf bifurcation is a local transition in which a complex-conjugate eigenvalue pair crosses the imaginary axis and a small periodic orbit is created or destroyed under nondegeneracy and transversality conditions. The resulting cycle's stability depends on whether the bifurcation is supercritical or subcritical.
required_concepts: Complex eigenvalue pair crosses zero real part.
Periodic-orbit birth or death requires the relevant nondegeneracy conditions.
accepted_variants: An oscillatory local bifurcation.
major_error_concepts: Inferring a Hopf bifurcation from any purely imaginary eigenvalues without checking crossing and nondegeneracy.

cards.prompt: What is Saddle–Node Bifurcation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A saddle-node bifurcation creates or destroys a pair of equilibria as a parameter crosses a threshold. The scalar normal form x' = mu - x squared has two equilibria for mu positive, one degenerate equilibrium at zero, and none for mu negative.
required_concepts: Collision or creation of two equilibria.
A zero eigenvalue occurs at the generic threshold.
accepted_variants: Fold bifurcation of equilibria.
major_error_concepts: Calling the appearance of a periodic orbit a saddle-node bifurcation of equilibria.

description: A definition-recall course deck covering core concepts in Ordinary Differential Equations.
